title: If a variable is `static`, does it take part in serialization (no — static belongs to the class, not the instance)?
shortTitle: If a variable is static, does it take part in serialization

s1_definition.profdef: No, static fields do not take part in serialization. Serialization captures the state of a specific instance, and a static field belongs to the class rather than to any instance, so the serialization engine skips it entirely. On deserialization the restored object simply reads whatever current value the static field holds in the running JVM, which means a static value is never written into the byte stream and is never restored from it, a frequent source of confusion when a static field appears to change after a round-trip.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a static field is like the branch's shared notice board showing today's base interest rate, which belongs to the whole branch, not to any single customer. Serialization seals Rajesh's personal account packet, which contains only his own details, so it never copies the shared notice board into his packet. When his packet is unfolded later, it just looks up at whatever the notice board currently says, which may have changed since the packet was sealed.
s1_definition.oneliner: Static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so serialization skips them; after deserialization a static field reflects the JVM's current value, not whatever it was when the object was serialized.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** No, static fields do not take part in serialization. Serialization captures the state of a specific instance, and a static field belongs to the class rather than to any instance, so the serialization engine skips it entirely. On deserialization the restored object simply reads whatever current value the static field holds in the running JVM, which means a static value is never written into the byte stream and is never restored from it, a frequent source of confusion when a static field appears to change after a round-trip.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, a static field is like the branch's shared notice board showing today's base interest rate, which belongs to the whole branch, not to any single customer. Serialization seals Rajesh's personal account packet, which contains only his own details, so it never copies the shared notice board into his packet. When his packet is unfolded later, it just looks up at whatever the notice board currently says, which may have changed since the packet was sealed.

**One line to remember:** Static fields belong to the class, not the instance, so serialization skips them; after deserialization a static field reflects the JVM's current value, not whatever it was when the object was serialized.

sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An account class kept the branch base interest rate as a static field. An account was serialized while the rate was 6.50, the rate was later updated to 7.25, and when the account was deserialized it showed 7.25, surprising a junior developer who expected 6.50. This is exactly the static-is-not-serialized behavior.

Problem 2 — The team confirmed that per-account data like balance, which is an instance field, was correctly frozen into the bytes and restored unchanged. This is exactly the contrast between instance state and class state.

The code defines an `Account` with a static base rate and instance fields, a `Store` for the byte round-trip, and a `StaticSerializationDemo` main class that serializes, changes the static field, deserializes, and shows the difference.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
static-serialization-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/core/
│       ├── Account.java                 (static baseRate + instance fields)
│       ├── Store.java                    (byte round-trip)
│       └── StaticSerializationDemo.java  (main)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/*.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.core.StaticSerializationDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is Rajesh's account with accountId SAV2001 and balance 1000000.00, plus a class-level static base rate of 6.50.

Step 1: The demo prints the starting state, showing the static base rate at 6.50 and the instance balance at 1000000.00.

Step 2: The Store serializes the account. The byte stream captures the instance fields accountId and balance only. The static base rate is not written because it belongs to the class, not the instance.

Step 3: The code changes the shared static base rate to 7.25. Because there is one shared static field, this change affects the whole class immediately.

Step 4: The Store deserializes the bytes. The instance balance is restored exactly as 1000000.00 because it was in the stream.

Step 5: Reading the static base rate now yields 7.25, the current value, not the 6.50 that was in effect when the object was serialized, which demonstrates that static state is never frozen into the bytes.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Before serialize: baseRate=6.50 balance=1000000.00
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: Changed static baseRate to 7.25
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: After deserialize: balance=1000000.00 (restored) baseRate=7.25 (current, not frozen)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CLASS-LEVEL                               INSTANCE-LEVEL
  Account.baseRate = 6.50                   Account(SAV2001, balance=1000000.00)
       │ (shared, NOT serialized)                │
       │                                         ▼
       │                                   Store.serialize() → byte[] {accountId, balance}
       │                                         │  (baseRate absent)
  change baseRate = 7.25  ◀── time passes ──     │
       │                                         ▼
       │                                   Store.deserialize()
       └──────── object reads CURRENT ─────→ balance=1000000.00 (restored)
                 baseRate = 7.25 (not 6.50)
```

```

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Account holds per-account state; shared rate is      │
  │     class-level config, deliberately not instance state  │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────────┐
  │           Account             │ Serializable
  │  - baseRate: BigDecimal       │ STATIC → NOT serialized

  1. serialize(rajesh)          → byte[]{accountId, balance}
  2. Account.baseRate = 7.25    → class-wide change
  3. deserialize(bytes)         → balance=1000000.00 restored
  4. read Account.baseRate      → 7.25 (current, never frozen)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
No, static variables do not take part in serialization. Serialization captures the state of one specific instance, and it writes the non-static, non-transient instance fields into the byte stream. A static field belongs to the class, not to any instance, so there is nothing instance-specific to write, and the engine simply skips it.

The practical consequence is a classic trap that I always call out. If a class has a static field like a shared base rate, and I serialize an object while the rate is six and a half percent, then change the rate, then deserialize, the restored object will see the new rate, not the old one. That is because the old static value was never stored in the bytes; the deserialized object just reads whatever the static field currently holds in the running JVM. This is correct behavior, but it surprises people who assume the whole object, including class-level data, is frozen into the stream.

I contrast this with instance fields like balance, which are written into the bytes and restored exactly. So the rule for design is simple: if a value must survive serialization with the object, it has to be an instance field; if it is genuinely class-wide configuration, keeping it static is correct precisely because each deserialized object should pick up the current configuration rather than a stale snapshot.

I also note that I never need to mark a static field transient, because it is already excluded for a different reason: transient excludes chosen instance state, while static is excluded because it is class state. The same applies to constants, which are static final and also do not travel in the bytes, so after a redeploy every deserialized object reflects the new constant. In my banking work this mental model prevented a real confusion where a base interest rate appeared to change after a cache reload, and I could explain immediately that the rate was static and therefore always read live, never frozen.
